title: The bread you keep
hook: Basil preached that bread you hoard belongs to the hungry

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basil's new city outside Caesarea, with rooms for travelers, the sick and the lepers. Your line was a city of mercy. Where might your hour go? Day seven hundred twenty-five.

"I will pull down my barns, and will build greater." That's a rich man talking to himself in one of Jesus's parables in Luke. His land has brought in a huge harvest, and his storage can't hold it. So he makes a plan: bigger barns, then rest, eat, drink, be merry. That same night, God tells him his life will be required of him, and asks whose all that grain will be now. Basil, the bishop who built the city of mercy, preached a whole sermon on that one sentence, and he started by counting the rich man's pronouns.
screen: `A HARVEST TOO BIG.` → `BIGGER BARNS.` → `THAT SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, Basil listens to the rich man's words. My fruits. My barns. My goods. My soul. Basil points out that he talks only to himself. He doesn't ask anyone. He doesn't look up from the pile. And Basil asks the question underneath: what is actually yours? You came into the world with nothing, and you'll leave with nothing. Where did all this come from? Second, a picture from everyday life in his city. Imagine, Basil says, someone who gets to the theater early, takes a seat, and then tries to keep everyone else out, as if a show meant for everyone belonged to him because he arrived first. That, he says, is what the rich do with what was given for all: they grab it first and then call it theirs. Third, the line that gives today its name. Basil says it plainly to his congregation. The bread you are keeping belongs to the hungry. The coat you have stored away belongs to the one who has none. The shoes going to waste in your house belong to the barefoot. The money you have buried belongs to the one in need. He's not saying a barn is evil, or that having things is a sin. He's saying that the extra, the part sitting idle while someone goes without, already has an owner. Fourth, why Catholics still read him. Catholic teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: the things of the earth are meant for everyone, and owning something carries a duty toward the people who need it. Basil's sermon said something close to it long before. Read that way, a barn can be a freezer, a pantry, a closet.
screen: `MY FRUITS, MY BARNS, MY GOODS.` · `THE SEAT IN THE THEATER.` · `THE BREAD BELONGS TO THE HUNGRY.` · `GOODS MEANT FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `THE HUNGRY OWN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen for the word my, the way Basil did. Settle, and breathe. Say over, silently, what's in your kitchen: my cans at the back, my rice nobody has opened, my fruit that will go soft before anyone eats it. Notice how the word sits. Then choose one thing that is, in Basil's words, bread you are keeping. Then picture where it could go today: a food pantry box, a neighbor, someone you pass on the street. If you pray, you can offer it to God before you offer it to them. The bell holds the time.
The bread you keep. Basil's warning that the extra you hold back already belongs to the hungry. Today's word.
Your line: the hungry own it. Today, give that one thing from your kitchen away before dinner. Day seven hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes often keep food collection boxes and run pantries, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: owning something carries a duty to people in need.

original.note: Greek: bread — the bread Basil says belongs to the hungry.

what it means: Basil says the extra you keep while others go without already belongs to the hungry.
what a scholar hears: a homily on Luke 12:18, with the theater-seat image, that later Catholic teaching on the universal destination of goods would echo.

notes: Bread/coat/shoes/money lines are paraphrased, not quoted: the familiar English wording is modern. Some scholars place the bread line in Basil's homily 'To the Rich' or note close parallels there; confirm the homily.
Theater-seat image and 'you came naked, you will leave naked' framing paraphrased from the same homily; confirm.
'Basil is one of the voices that teaching has listened to' is interpretive; confirm whether Church documents cite Basil on this point, or soften.
Luke 12:18 Douay-Rheims quotation; confirm exact Challoner wording.
